issues.what: T1 is the overall task pasted verbatim ("The given image circulated with the following claim: ... state what could not be determined.") with no decomposition or ordered sub-goals (reverse search, caption/source check, compare).
issues.why_bad_to_teach: Teaches the coordinator to forward the case text instead of stating what the workspace must establish.
issues.ideal: One task is fine, but phrase it as concrete sub-goals: reverse-search E1, identify pages that caption the same picture, compare the best candidate's image to E1, compare with Joshimath reference photos.

issues.what: READ_RECORD E9 with rationale "reading E9's page text will reveal whether this image appears in the 2021 Uttarakhand disaster article and what location or caption is given"; E9 is the image record (the page is E10), and the read returned only width/height/source_url.
issues.why_bad_to_teach: Teaches confusing image records with page records and spending a step on a reference image the rationale already said does not match E1.
issues.ideal: Skip it and go straight to the reverse image search on E1, or read E10 if the caption of the reference was actually needed.

issues.what: Rationale says E34 holds "the landslide image found in search results, which appears to match Material A", but R17 came from a text search with no image or thumbnail fetched and no comparison, so nothing visible shows it matches.
issues.why_bad_to_teach: Teaches asserting a visual match for a page whose picture has not been seen.
issues.ideal: Say that the SERC page carries the same Cusco 2018 caption as R6/R7 and is a candidate whose image still has to be fetched and compared.

issues.what: READ_RECORD E1 justified as "Reading E1's metadata directly will formally document its origin and properties"; the record holds only filename/media_type/byte_size, which cannot document origin. The L3b rule's purpose (look at the reference photos again before reporting) is not stated.
issues.why_bad_to_teach: Teaches that file metadata establishes provenance, and teaches a rationale that does not match the rule's real purpose.
issues.ideal: Rationale: look at E1 next to the Joshimath references E9/E4/E7 once more before writing the reference-comparison finding.

issues.what: F1-F4 all repeat the same point ("matches a picture that ... SERC labels 'Landslide in Cusco, Peru 2018'", "supported location is Cusco", "source relied upon ... SERC", "establishes a matching published photograph and its Cusco attribution"), each citing [E34, E40]. This looks like a template filled in once per requirement.
issues.why_bad_to_teach: Teaches padding a report with near-duplicate findings instead of one finding per distinct fact.
issues.ideal: Merge them into one finding (match + caption + source URL) plus one finding that lists what is undetermined.

issues.what: The Cusco attribution rests only on SERC (E34). Other visible corroboration goes uncited: the near-identical reverse-search hits R6/R7 captioned "A landslide near Cusco, Peru, in 2018" (page E19 was read), and R18 "A landslide near Cusco, Peru, March 2018. Image via Wikimedia Commons". The limitation "2 of 5 candidate pages failed to load" sits under the compare finding F6 and does not say that the failed page was the Wikimedia Commons file page, the likely original.
issues.why_bad_to_teach: Teaches citing one page when several independent ones agree, and leaving it unsaid that the likely original source was lost to a tool failure.
issues.ideal: Cite E34 plus E19 (and R18's snippet record) for the caption, and state that the Commons file page (R16), probably the original upload, failed to load, so the photographer and original date are still open.

issues.what: Both rationales open with the same template sentence, "E1 shows a green mountainside with large fissures", before moving on.
issues.why_bad_to_teach: Mechanical repeated wording makes rationales boilerplate rather than tied to each step.
issues.ideal: Each rationale should state only what is new at that step (e.g. 'references don't match, so reverse-search E1').

good_patterns: Runs a reverse image search on E1 early, follows the caption it surfaces (Cusco 2018), then fetches the candidate page's main image and runs compare_media before relying on the attribution.
Report and answer word the result as a published attribution ('SERC labels ...', 'published location') and explicitly decline to treat the title year as the capture date.
Honest about the reference-photo comparison: says it cannot establish Joshimath, and that different viewpoints alone cannot prove a different place.
Reports the compare_media result with its threshold caveat (no difference above min_area 0.0005) instead of claiming the copies are unedited.
cannot_judge: Whether E34's truncated content (+817 chars) names 'Carleton College' or gives an original source or date; F1's 'Carleton College' may otherwise be inferred only from the URL.
Whether E19's truncated page text (+5678 chars) contains the Cusco 2018 caption next to the matching picture.
Whether the visual descriptions of E9/E4/E7 in F5 (e.g. E7 as 'a snowy settlement and a separate cracked paved surface') are accurate; the images themselves are not rendered here.
Whether 'after alignment' in F6 appears on the E40 evidence card; the visible observation shows only 'measured 0.000%'.
summary: A solid location-debunk trajectory: reverse image search finds near-identical copies captioned as a 2018 Cusco, Peru landslide; the SERC page's image is fetched and compared pixel-for-pixel with E1; and the answer gives a correctly hedged 'misleading, published location Cusco' verdict with capture date and exact site left open. The issues are all minor: a verbatim plan; two filler reads (the E9 image record, and E1's metadata with a rationale claiming it documents origin); one rationale claiming a match before any comparison; template-like duplicate findings F1-F4; and the Cusco attribution resting on one source although other pages corroborate it, with no explicit note that the Commons original failed to load. Nothing here would teach hallucination or a wrong verdict.
